title: Design a parking lot
prompt: Design the classes for a multi-level parking lot that parks vehicles of different sizes and charges for time parked.
clarify: Which vehicle types and spot sizes exist, and can a small vehicle use a large spot?
How is pricing computed (per hour, tiers, per vehicle type)?
Do we need to handle multiple entrances and exits concurrently?
strongAnswer: Identifies the core entities: ParkingLot, Level, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket and a pricing component.
Separates responsibilities: spot allocation, ticketing and fee calculation are different concerns.
Uses a Strategy for pricing and for spot-selection rules, so new rules do not change existing classes.
Models spot size compatibility explicitly rather than with scattered conditionals.
Handles concurrency: two cars must not get the same spot, so allocation is atomic.
Describes how to test fee calculation and allocation in isolation.
pitfalls: One giant class that does everything.
Switch statements on vehicle type everywhere.
Ignoring concurrent entrances.

title: Design an LRU cache
prompt: Implement a fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used entry, with get and put in constant time.
clarify: What happens when capacity is reached and on update of an existing key?
Must it be thread-safe?
Do entries need expiry as well?
strongAnswer: Combines a hash map with a doubly linked list so lookup and reordering are both O(1).
On get, moves the node to the front; on put, inserts at the front and evicts from the tail when over capacity.
Handles updates of existing keys and capacity edge cases such as capacity one.
Explains how to make it thread-safe (a lock, or sharded locks) and the throughput trade-off.
Mentions extensions: time-based expiry, other eviction policies behind an interface.
Lists tests: ordering after gets, eviction order, updates and capacity limits.
pitfalls: Using only a list or only a map and getting O(n) operations.
Forgetting to refresh recency on get.
Ignoring thread safety when asked.

title: Design an elevator system
prompt: Design the control logic for a building with several elevators that serves requests from floors and from inside the cars.
clarify: How many elevators and floors, and is there a peak-hour pattern?
What scheduling goal matters: waiting time, energy or fairness?
Do we handle emergencies and out-of-service cars?
strongAnswer: Models Elevator, Request (hall call and car call), Direction and a central Dispatcher.
Represents each elevator as a state machine (idle, moving up, moving down, doors open).
Chooses a scheduling approach such as serving requests in the current direction first, and assigns hall calls to the best elevator using a cost function.
Keeps scheduling behind a Strategy interface so policies can change.
Handles edge cases: requests arriving while moving, the same floor requested twice and a failed car.
Discusses how to simulate and test the dispatcher deterministically.
pitfalls: Handling every request in arrival order.
Mixing hardware control and scheduling logic.
No model of direction.

title: Design a rate limiter class
prompt: Write a rate limiter component for a single server that allows at most N requests per user per time window, designed so the algorithm can change.
clarify: Which algorithm and what happens on rejection?
Per user, per key or global?
Must it be thread-safe and how many users are there?
strongAnswer: Defines a small interface such as allow(key) and implements token bucket and sliding window behind it (Strategy).
Tracks state per key in a map with cleanup for idle keys so memory does not grow without bound.
Computes token refill lazily from elapsed time instead of using a background thread.
Makes the clock injectable so tests are deterministic.
Handles concurrency with per-key locking or atomic operations rather than one global lock.
Explains how it would extend to a distributed store.
pitfalls: Using real time inside the class, which makes tests flaky.
One global lock that serialises all users.
Never evicting state for idle keys.

title: Fix failing tests in an unfamiliar codebase with an assistant
prompt: You are given a small multi-file project with several failing tests and an AI assistant. Get the tests passing and explain your changes.
clarify: Which tests should I start with and may I run them freely?
Which files may I change?
Is the assistant allowed for all tasks or only some?
strongAnswer: Reads the test names and failures first and builds a mental model of the code before prompting.
States a hypothesis for each failure and checks it, instead of asking the assistant to fix everything.
Uses the assistant for small, specific help (explain this function, draft a test) and reviews each answer.
Runs the tests after every change and keeps changes minimal and explained.
Notices and corrects at least one wrong suggestion and says so.
Finishes by summarising the root causes and what remains risky.
pitfalls: Pasting all failures and applying the answer unread.
Changing many files before running a test.
Staying silent while prompting.

title: Extend an existing feature in stages with an assistant
prompt: You are given a working program and asked to add features in three stages (for example new rules, then new cases, then performance), with an assistant available.
clarify: What are the exact requirements for each stage?
Are there performance targets?
Should earlier behaviour remain unchanged?
strongAnswer: Plans the data structure and approach for each stage before generating code.
Delegates boilerplate and test generation but writes or closely reviews the core logic.
Adds tests first for new behaviour and confirms existing tests still pass.
Notices when a naive suggestion is too slow and explains the complexity problem.
Keeps functions small so each piece can be reviewed and explained.
Explains clearly what was delegated and why.
pitfalls: Letting the assistant restructure the whole program.
Not rechecking earlier stages after later changes.
Accepting an O(n squared) approach without checking constraints.

title: Tell me about a mistake or failure
prompt: Tell me about a time something you built or decided did not work out. What happened and what did you do?
clarify: Is a personal or academic project acceptable?
How much detail should I give about the technical cause?
strongAnswer: Picks a real failure with stakes, not a disguised strength.
Explains the context and what you expected to happen.
Owns the decision and the root cause without blaming others.
Describes what you did to fix it and to reduce the chance of repeating it.
States a concrete lesson and, if possible, a later example where you applied it.
pitfalls: Choosing a trivial or fake weakness.
Blaming teammates or tools.
Ending without a lesson.

title: Tell me about a technical disagreement
prompt: Describe a time you disagreed with a teammate about a technical decision. How was it resolved?
clarify: Should the example be recent?
May I describe a decision where I turned out to be wrong?
strongAnswer: Explains both positions fairly, including the strongest argument for the other side.
Describes how you gathered evidence (a benchmark, a prototype, a written comparison) instead of arguing opinions.
Shows respect and listening, and how the decision was finally made.
States the outcome, whether you were right, and how the relationship was afterwards.
Reflects on what you would do differently.
pitfalls: Painting the other person as unreasonable.
No evidence, only persistence.
A story where you simply won.

title: Tell me about a vague or ambiguous project
prompt: Tell me about a project where the requirements were unclear. How did you make progress?
clarify: Does it matter if the project was small?
Should I focus on the technical or the organisational side?
strongAnswer: Describes what was ambiguous and the cost of getting it wrong.
Shows how you reduced ambiguity: questions to stakeholders, a small prototype or a written assumptions list.
Explains how you made decisions with incomplete information and what you deferred.
Gives the outcome with a measurable result.
Reflects on how you would clarify earlier next time.
pitfalls: Waiting passively for clarity.
Building everything before checking assumptions.
A story without a result.

title: How do you use AI tools in your work?
prompt: Describe how you use AI coding tools in a typical project, and give an example of where they got something wrong.
clarify: Which tools am I allowed to talk about?
Should I focus on coding, testing or design?
strongAnswer: Says what is delegated (boilerplate, test scaffolding, unfamiliar syntax) and what is kept (design, tricky logic, review).
Explains the verification habit: reading the diff, running tests and checking against documentation.
Gives a specific example of an AI mistake, how it was caught and what it cost.
Shows awareness of limits such as security, licensing and confidential data.
Avoids both extremes: not using it at all, or trusting it blindly.
pitfalls: Claiming it writes all your code.
Claiming you never use it.
No concrete example.
